Patrick Clancy has endured the kind of loss no father should ever face.
Now, after a Massachusetts jury failed to reach a verdict in the case against his former wife, Lindsay Clancy, he is confronting the possibility of going through the entire ordeal again.
His response was not a victory speech. It was a statement about grief that has no finish line.
Through attorney David Meier, Patrick thanked the judge and jurors for their work before addressing what another trial would mean for him and his family.
Meier said the loss of Patrick’s children is something from which he will never recover and for which there will never be closure.
He added that reliving the tragedy through another trial would be extraordinarily painful.
Patrick Clancy After Mistrial: “Will Have to Relive the Pain” of Children’s Deaths https://t.co/jFkKPOxIMC pic.twitter.com/BBtkDb9Amp
— LifeNews.com (@LifeNewsHQ) September 5, 2026
The children were Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, just 8 months old.
They were killed inside the family’s Duxbury home on January 24, 2023.
Lindsay Clancy admitted killing the children but pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. She remains charged with three counts of first-degree murder, and the mistrial was neither a conviction nor an acquittal.
Fox News, The Associated Press, and WBUR reported that Judge William Sullivan declared the mistrial Friday after jurors could not unanimously decide whether Lindsay Clancy was criminally responsible for the children’s deaths.
The six-week trial ended after more than 38 hours of deliberations across seven days, with reporting describing an 11-1 split in favor of acquittal on the criminal-responsibility question.
Prosecutors argued that Clancy understood her actions and deliberately sent Patrick out on errands, while the defense said postpartum psychosis left her unable to appreciate the wrongfulness of what she did.
Jurors sent multiple notes about the impasse, and the defense unsuccessfully sought to have the lone juror removed before Sullivan ended the proceeding and discharged the panel.
A judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial declared a mistrial Friday after jurors failed to reach a verdict in a case that sharply divided many Americans over whether the Massachusetts woman should be criminally responsible for killing her three young children. pic.twitter.com/E8Fz8vDfEP
— The Associated Press (@AP) September 4, 2026
The central issue was not whether Lindsay Clancy caused the children’s deaths. It was whether Massachusetts law allowed the jury to hold her criminally responsible at the time.
The official Plymouth County indictment charged her with three counts of murder and three counts of strangulation after a grand jury reviewed the case in 2023.
Those charges remain pending because a hung jury does not end a prosecution or resolve guilt, and prosecutors may legally place the same criminal-responsibility question before a new jury in a second trial.
Clancy continues to be held without bail at Tewksbury Hospital, a forensic psychiatric facility, while the court and prosecutors determine what comes next after weeks of testimony and seven days of deliberations.
A status hearing is scheduled for September 29, when the judge may address the defense’s pending motion and the possibility of assigning a new trial date.
Until then, the case remains in a pretrial posture, and any choice to seek a second jury belongs to the Plymouth County District Attorney’s Office.
After the judge declared a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial on Friday, Plymouth District Attorney Tim Cruz emphasized that the case was about getting justice for the child victims — Cora, Dawson and Callan.
"It is our job to make sure that the victims are not… pic.twitter.com/HdE0khbUrX
— CBS News (@CBSNews) September 4, 2026
There are legal questions still to answer. Prosecutors must decide whether to retry the case, pursue another resolution, or take a different path.
But Patrick Clancy’s statement cuts through all of that.
No ruling can bring Cora, Dawson, and Callan home. No second jury can give their father closure.

President Donald Trump said Lindsay Clancy will still have to pay “the price” for the deaths of her three small children — Cora 5, Dawson 3, and Callan, 8 months — after a mistrial was ruled on Friday.
During a press gaggle in the Oval Office, a reporter asked Trump if he’d been following the murder trial of Clancy, a Massachusetts mom whose defense did not deny that she strangled her children with exercise bands in January 2023, but argued that she was not guilty by reason of insanity. Her attorneys claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis, a severe but rare psychiatric condition in which a person is disconnected from reality.
“It’s a horrible tragedy,” Trump shared with reporters. “It’s a horrible tragedy. I see what’s happened, and it looks like it’s a hung jury.”
“I assume there’s going to be another trial. It’s a terrible situation. Look, she did a horrible, horrible thing. Can’t be worse. But you’ll find out what the price to pay is. There’ll be a price. It’s going to be [a] mental institution or jail or something,” Trump continued.
LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL DECLARED AFTER JURY DEADLOCKS IN KILLINGS OF HER THREE CHILDREN
The six-week trial, which was supposed to determine whether Clancy was to be held criminally responsible, quickly evolved into a flashpoint in the internet culture war over women’s postpartum mental health and spurred misinformation and conspiracy theories, including false claims accusing her ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, of being responsible for the children’s deaths.
After nearly a week of deliberations, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial when the jury deadlocked 11 to 1: 11 jurors voted to acquit Clancy, while one holdout refused to join them. The jury consisted of 9 women and 3 men.
Clancy’s defense attorney requested that the lone juror be removed because a note given to the judge by the jurors said the holdout had doubt but refused to apply it, according to People.
The mistrial invoked a strong reaction from Republican lawmakers, while Democratic lawmakers and leaders — including those from Clancy’s state — have remained mum on the high-profile case.
“Out of 12 people, only ONE had the courage to hold a serial killer accountable for her actions,” Rep. Michael Rulli, R-Ohio, posted on X. “That’s not just bravery. That’s a hero.”
“Holdout juror’s going to need security,” Sen. Mike Lee, R-Ohio, posted on X. “Sad.”
Florida Republican Governor Ron DeSantis called the mistrial a “miscarriage of justice.”
“The victims deserved far, far better than a kangaroo court,” DeSantis wrote.
Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., who has been incredibly vocal against Clancy’s supporters — who have been gathered outside the courthouse and posted videos showing support online — suggesting Clancy would not have this support if she were Black.
“This case is not about the excuses for why she committed murder,” Mace posted on X. “This is about justice for the three beautiful souls whose lives were taken after their mother strangled them with her bare hands and workout bands.”
“12 jurors looked at this onesie,” Mace continued. “Only ONE stood his ground to defend the children.”
But Clancy’s defense argued that she was a devoted and loving mother who was desperately seeking to get help, alleging that the cocktail of medications she was on worsened her mental state. Clancy had been prescribed 13 psychiatric medications — more than 30 prescriptions — in the four months leading up to the murders.
Patrick Clancy is suing for wrongful death and medical malpractice against Clancy’s providers, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, Rebecca Jollotta, Aster Mental Health and South Shore Health System. Clancy also filed a separate lawsuit alleging negligence, medical malpractice and personal injury.
“Lindsay was struggling. We were all very concerned,” Susan Clancy, Clancy’s mother-in-law, told jurors. “She was very nurturing, very loving. She was a wonderful mother. Wonderful.”
Clancy is due back in court Sept. 29 for a status hearing, trial assignment and a defense Rule 25 motion.

Psychosis
Evil Deeds and Dangerous States of Mind
Why the insanity defense is complicated, uncommon, and so difficult to prove.
Updated September 6, 2026 Reviewed by Margaret Foley
Key points
- The insanity defense relies on the defendant's mental state at the time of the crime, not at trial.
- Psychosis is unpredictable, with biological and non-biological triggers that can strike at any stage of life.
- The case illustrates the challenge of proving a defendant's prior mental state beyond a reasonable doubt.
This is Part 2 of a series about the Lindsay Clancy case. Read Part 1 here.
The so-called insanity defense, or LCR (lack of criminal responsibility) as it is called in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, differs from determining a defendant's competency to stand trial, which is about their current mental status. Instead, it hinges on the defendant's state of mind at the moment the crime was committed, which, in some cases, can be years or even decades ago. When conducting forensic evaluations for the insanity defense, determining (or trying to reconstruct) the defendant's state of mind before, during, and immediately following the criminal offense is absolutely essential. What was Ms. Clancy's condition during this time period? Perhaps most crucially, was she psychotic?
What is Psychosis?
Psychosis is the most debilitating of all psychiatric disorders. If truth be told, no one really knows where psychosis comes from or what causes it. Psychosis appears to have some genetic basis and can run in families, though this is not always the case. And though the chance of identical (monozygotic) twins raised in similar or the same environments both suffering from a psychotic disorder such as schizophrenia is fairly high (up to 50 percent to 70 percent), it is still not 100 percent, indicating there are other significant factors beyond biology and genetics at play. Some of those factors are psychological stress, substance abuse, and emotional trauma. I have worked with psychotic patients for many years, and it's clear that there is a significant psychological component to this complex and devastating mental state and that it is an archetypal human experience to which none of us is totally immune. The frightening fact of the matter is that people can become psychotic with or without a genetic history of the disorder and at any stage of life, especially during periods of extreme biopsychosocial stress.
What Was Clancy's State of Mind at the Time of the Killings?
For me, the key question here has to do with whether or not the defendant was psychotic at the time she committed the killings. Postpartum depression is not the same as postpartum psychosis. Most of the mental health professionals who evaluated Ms. Clancy, including her treating psychiatrist, did not note any psychotic signs or symptoms during the period prior to the offense. Nor does she seem to exhibit psychotic symptomatology at present. However, one forensic psychologist who treated her at a hospital following the crime diagnosed her as suffering from both postpartum psychosis and bipolar disorder, stating that she feared others could hear her thoughts, a classic psychotic symptom called "thought broadcasting." The assertion that Ms. Clancy told another forensic evaluator, her hospital chaplain, and her husband about having heard a persistent disembodied male voice commanding her to kill her kids and herself before doing so, something clinically called a "command hallucination," is certainly possible but also somewhat suspicious. Malingering or lying by the defendant about such things would not be unusual in such a high-stakes case.
It is essential to keep in mind that Lindsay Clancy was an experienced labor and delivery nurse, had almost certainly seen postpartum and other kinds of psychosis before, and conceivably may have realized that unless she could convince the jury that she experienced psychotic symptoms such as command hallucinations, it would be considerably more challenging for her lawyers to prevail. (This is especially true under Massachusetts law, which requires the state to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that she was not too debilitated by her mental state to be held criminally responsible.)
It would now appear that the lone juror who forced Ms. Clancy's mistrial did so because he apparently believed that the prosecution had sufficiently demonstrated the defendant's guilt and criminal responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt, rejecting the defense team's claim of lack of criminal responsibility (LCR). This seems a reasonable position, especially if the defendant was not convincingly shown to be psychotic at the time of the crime. On the other hand, if Ms. Clancy was telling the truth about having experienced command hallucinations and thought broadcasting before or during the commission of this offense, that would have proved sufficient to win her case in my opinion. So this is, for me, a central point. Time will tell—if there is another trial.
From what has been publicly reported, it sounds as though, at the very least, Ms. Clancy suffered from severe depressive symptoms before, during, and immediately after the killings, when she attempted to commit suicide by superficially slashing her wrists and neck and then jumping out of a two-story window, causing her to become paralyzed from the waist down. (This appears to have been more of a legitimate attempt than a manipulative suicide gesture, though it is highly likely that a registered nurse like Clancy would know how to cut their wrists if they really wanted to die.) Prior to the murders, she had evidently consulted numerous clinicians, including psychiatrists, psychotherapists, and psychiatric nurse practitioners, regarding symptoms such as acute insomnia, sadness, and anxiety, had been briefly psychiatrically hospitalized, and was prescribed numerous psychotropic medications intended to ameliorate her symptoms.
According to her mother, who is also a nurse but not a mental health professional, Ms. Clancy was "paranoid" during this period, but it is not clear what she meant by this. Clinically, this term paranoia refers to paranoid or persecutory delusions or fixed, irrational beliefs, which, if they were indeed present around and during the time of the murders, would support the argument that Clancy was psychotic. But this was not emphasized at trial. Did Clancy become delusional during that period? By definition, true paranoia includes delusions of some sort, e.g., the patient fearing the CIA, FBI, etc., is spying on them or that people in general are against them and trying to deliberately harm or trick them. Ms. Clancy's reported fear of sleeping alone or that her psychiatric medications were "destroying her mind" does not, in and of itself, rise to the definition of clinical paranoia, by definition, a psychotic symptom. There was also some evidence presented indicating that she had probably been thinking of killing her children and perhaps herself for some time, citing searches on her computer or phone asking, for instance, whether the airbags in her car could be disabled and how to locate the carotid artery.
Conclusion
In most insanity cases here in California, which, unlike in Massachusetts, need to be proven by the defense by a preponderance of the evidence, a lower bar, rather than beyond a reasonable doubt, without more convincing proof of the presence of psychotic symptoms such as delusions or auditory, visual, or other hallucinations, it seems unlikely to me that a jury would find that the severe symptoms of depression and anxiety alone, though clearly painful, were sufficiently debilitating to impair a defendant's reality testing, insight, and judgment to the point of being unable to appreciate the criminality or wrongfulness of their conduct or to have been, as a result of said mental disease or defect, unable to conform their conduct to the requirements of the law, as required in Massachusetts. Suicide is one thing. Filicide is another. For a mother to calculatingly and coldly strangle her own children to death and be excused, acquitted, or found not guilty for doing so by a jury of her peers requires, it seems to me, a higher burden of proof.

What Does Mistrial Mean? Lindsay Clancy's Ex-Husband Breaks His Silence Over 'Extraordinarily Painful' Retrial
After a jury could not agree, Lindsay Clancy's case remains unresolved, leaving a grieving family facing the deeply painful prospect of another trial
A mistrial was declared in Lindsay Clancy's murder case at Plymouth County Superior Court in Massachusetts on Friday, 4 September, after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict following seven days of deliberations. Her ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, later said through his attorney that the prospect of another trial over their three children's deaths would be 'extraordinarily painful.'
The ruling ended the trial without a verdict but did not end the criminal case. Clancy, 36, remains charged with murder and is expected to remain at a psychiatric hospital while the proceedings continue. Prosecutors have not yet announced whether they will seek a second trial.
What Does a Mistrial Mean in the Lindsay Clancy Case?
A mistrial occurs when a trial cannot be completed with a valid verdict. In this case, Judge William Sullivan declared one after jurors repeatedly reported that they could not unanimously agree on whether Clancy was criminally responsible for killing her children.
A mistrial following a deadlocked jury is neither a conviction nor an acquittal. The charges remain pending, and prosecutors may seek another trial. The defence also has a Rule 25 motion pending, which asks the judge for a required finding of not guilty on the ground that the evidence was legally insufficient to sustain a conviction.
Clancy does not dispute that she killed Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months old, at the family's Duxbury home on 24 January 2023. She pleaded not guilty, and her defence argued that postpartum psychosis left her not criminally responsible under Massachusetts law.
Under Massachusetts law, criminal responsibility is a legal question rather than simply a medical diagnosis. Once the issue is properly raised, prosecutors must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was criminally responsible. A person is not criminally responsible if, because of a mental disease or defect, they lacked the substantial capacity to appreciate the criminality or wrongfulness of their conduct or to conform their conduct to the law.
Prosecutors argued that Clancy acted deliberately and remained able to understand and control her actions. The defence maintained that her mental illness deprived her of criminal responsibility.
Patrick Clancy Speaks After Mistrial
Hours after Sullivan declared the mistrial, attorney David Meier released a statement on Patrick Clancy's behalf thanking the court and jurors for their work.
The statement said the loss of Patrick's children was something from which he would never recover and that there would never be closure. It added that the prospect of reliving the tragedy through another trial was 'extraordinarily painful' for Patrick and his family.
The statement did not urge prosecutors either to retry the case or to abandon it. Patrick had previously spoken publicly about Lindsay, including asking people to forgive her after the children's deaths. He also testified as the prosecution's first witness during the trial.
During his testimony, Patrick described leaving the family home on 24 January 2023 to pick up medicine for one of the children and collect takeaway food. When he returned, he found Lindsay injured outside the house and later discovered the children in the basement.
Jury Deadlock and What Happens Next
The jury told the court three times that it could not reach a unanimous decision. During the final phase of deliberations, the foreperson reported concerns that one juror was not applying the court's reasonable-doubt instructions as other jurors believed they should be applied.
Defence attorney Kevin Reddington sought further questioning or removal of that juror. Sullivan declined to intervene further in the deliberations. The defence then sought emergency relief from the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court to delay the mistrial declaration and pursue further inquiry, but the request was denied.
Sullivan subsequently declared the mistrial, leaving the prosecution unresolved. Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said there would not be an immediate decision on whether to retry Clancy.
Clancy is due back in court on 29 September for a status hearing, trial assignment and consideration of the Rule 25 motion. Sullivan has indicated that, if another trial is pursued, he would prefer it to take place 'sooner rather than later,' although no retrial date has been set.
